what_it_does: Graph-processing software (think: finding friends-of-friends in a social network or ranking web pages) has an irregular structure where some nodes connect to thousands of neighbors while others connect to just a few. On a GPU — which runs many threads in lock-step groups called warps — this means some threads in a group finish quickly while others are still plodding through a densely connected node, wasting the idle threads' time. SparseWeaver proposes treating these irregular sparse graph operations as if they were regular dense operations, so all threads in a group stay busy. It does this by adding a small, lightweight piece of extra circuitry inside the GPU's processing core that detects the imbalance pattern and restructures the work on the fly, using the graph's own connectivity structure to guide the rebalancing without adding extra memory or synchronization cost. The design is validated on an open-source research GPU called Vortex that runs on a RISC-V instruction set.
